When you're the lawyer, the billing department, and the collections team rolled into one, time entry becomes the task that always gets pushed to tomorrow.


The right billing software changes that equation entirely. This guide breaks down what to look for, compares the top options for 2026, and shows you how to calculate whether a new tool will actually pay for itself.


## What is legal billing software for solo attorneys


For solo attorneys in 2026, the best legal billing software options are cloud-based, automated solutions designed to maximize billable hours while remaining easy to use. Top choices include platforms like Clio for comprehensive practice management, LeanLaw for QuickBooks integration, and AI-native tools like PointOne for automated time capture.


So what exactly is legal billing software?


It's a system that helps attorneys track billable time, generate invoices, process payments, and manage trust accounts — all in one place. Unlike generic invoicing tools, legal billing software addresses requirements specific to law practice: Interest on Lawyer Trust Accounts (IOLTA) compliance, matter-based billing, Outside Counsel Guidelines (OCGs), and[LEDES (Legal Electronic Data Exchange Standard)](https://pointone.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-utbms-codes) .


A typical billing platform handles five core functions:


-


**Time tracking:** Recording billable and non-billable hours by client matter


-


**Invoice generation:** Creating compliant invoices from recorded time and expenses


-


**Payment processing:** Accepting credit cards and ACH through legal-compliant processors


-


**Trust accounting:** Managing IOLTA accounts with proper fund separation


-


**Reporting:** Providing visibility into collections, realization rates, and receivables


## Why solo attorneys benefit from dedicated billing software


Generic tools and manual methods — spreadsheets, paper timesheets, Word templates — create compounding problems for solo practitioners. You're simultaneously the timekeeper, the biller, and the collections department. Without dedicated software, billable time goes unrecorded, invoices go out late, and payments slow down because clients lack convenient ways to pay.


The most common pain points?


Reconstructing time from memory at week's end. Delayed invoicing because billing always loses to client work. Payment friction when clients can only pay by check. Compliance risk from inconsistent trust fund handling. Dedicated billing software addresses each of these directly.


## Key features to look for in solo attorney billing software


### Automated time tracking and passive time capture


The biggest revenue problem for solos isn't inaccurate time — it's time that isn't consistently recorded. While manual timers are standard,[passive time capture](https://pointone.com/blog/what-is-ai-time-tracking) changes the equation entirely. AI-native tools can record work activity across email, documents, and calls, then generate draft time entries automatically. Your role shifts from data entry to quick review.


### Invoice generation and attorney invoicing tools


Your law firm invoicing software produces[professional, compliant invoices](https://pointone.com/blog/how-to-craft-better-legal-bills) without manual formatting. Look for customizable templates, expense attachment capabilities, and support for different[billing arrangements](https://pointone.com/attorneyintelligence/the-billable-hour-is-not-dying-it-s-mutating/) : hourly, flat fee, contingency, and hybrid models.


### Trust and IOLTA accounting compliance


Most state bars require strict separation of client funds in an IOLTA. Billing software for attorneys handles three-way reconciliation — matching the trust journal, client ledgers, and bank statement. For a solo without a dedicated bookkeeper, having this built in is essential.


### Online payment processing


Offering clients online payment options dramatically accelerates collections. However, legal payment software complies with bar rules, particularly regarding how processing fees are handled and ensuring they aren't deducted from trust deposits. The best solutions also support next-day deposits.


### E-billing and outside counsel guideline compliance


E-billing isn't just an enterprise concern anymore. Solos working with insurance companies or corporate clients increasingly submit invoices in LEDES format and follow strict billing rules. Legal e-billing software automates compliance checks, preventing rejections and payment delays.


### Integrations with practice management and accounting systems


Your billing software connects seamlessly with your practice management system (Clio, Filevine), accounting software (QuickBooks, Xero), and email client. The best tools layer on top of existing systems rather than forcing a rip-and-replace.


### Reporting and revenue analytics


Essential reports include outstanding accounts receivable, collections by matter, realization rates (the percentage of billed time actually collected), and utilization metrics. Realization rate, by the way, is simply how much of what you bill actually gets paid—a key indicator of billing health.

## How much billing software for solo attorneys costs


Pricing models vary: per-user monthly subscriptions, flat monthly fees, percentage of collections (common for payment processing), and free tiers with significant limitations. The cheapest option is rarely the best value — consider total cost of ownership, including time spent on manual workarounds.


-


**Free and ultra-budget options:** Basic invoicing with limited features, often lacking trust accounting or integrations


-


**Mid-range options:** Full billing workflows, online payments, and essential reporting — the sweet spot for many solos


-


**Premium options:** AI-powered time capture, compliance automation, in-depth analytics, and priority support


When evaluating cost, calculate the value of recovered billable time against the monthly fee. For most solos, revenue recovered from more complete time capture exceeds the software cost.


## How AI is changing legal billing for solo practitioners


A significant shift is underway from["AI-enabled" software](https://pointone.com/attorneyintelligence/the-ai-adoption-illusion/) (features bolted onto legacy architecture) to "AI-native" platforms (built from the ground up around AI). For solos, this means moving from manually entering time to simply reviewing and approving entries captured automatically.


What does AI actually do in billing software? Here's what's now possible:


-


**Passive activity capture:** Recording work across email, documents, calls, and web activity without starting timers


-


**Context-aware classification:** Automatically matching activities to the correct client and matter


-


**Narrative generation:** Drafting compliant time entry descriptions from raw activity data


-


**Compliance automation:** Checking entries against firm policies and client guidelines before submission


-


**Voice-to-entry:** Converting dictated notes into structured, multi-matter time entries

## How to calculate the ROI of billing software


Rather than guessing, walk through the logic:


1.


**Estimate unrecorded time:** How many hours per week go unrecorded due to entry friction or forgetting to start timers?


2.


**Calculate the revenue gap:** Multiply lost hours by your effective billing rate.


3.


**Estimate invoicing speed:** How many days faster could you send invoices with automation?


4.


**Factor in faster collections:** Quantify the value of reduced receivables float.


5.


**Calculate net impact:** Subtract monthly software cost from recovered revenue.


For most solos, recovered revenue from more complete time capture alone covers the software cost multiple times over.


## How to choose the right billing software for your practice


Start by auditing your current process. The answers highlight which features matter most for your situation.


-


How do you track time now?


-


When do invoices go out?


-


Where does the process break down?


Next, consider your practice area and what's most important for you: contingency tracking, LEDES compliance, flexible flat-fee billing. The perfect software will meet you where you are.


Then verify integrations actually work. Don't accept vendor claims at face value — ask for a demo showing connections to your practice management system, accounting software, and email. Even if you're solo today, choose software that grows with you. A platform that scales from one user to a multi-attorney firm prevents painful migrations later.


Finally, look beyond the monthly sticker price. Factor in implementation time, training, integration costs, and the hidden cost of manual workarounds with a less capable tool.

## Frequently asked questions


What is the best billing system for solo lawyers who handle personal injury cases?


Personal injury solos benefit from software supporting contingency fee tracking, expense advancement logging, and settlement disbursement sheets. All-in-one tools like Clio and Smokeball handle personal injury workflows well, while PointOne captures all related activity even when hourly billing isn't the primary model.


Can solo attorneys use billing software if they bill on contingency instead of hourly?


Yes, most modern legal billing software supports multiple fee arrangements including contingency, flat fee, and hybrid billing. The depth of contingency-specific features varies by platform, so verify this capability before committing.


How does legal billing software handle split billing across multiple matters?


Most attorney billing programs allow a single time entry or expense to be allocated across multiple matters or clients. The software calculates each party's share automatically, eliminating manual calculations.


Do solo attorneys benefit from e-billing software for insurance defense work?


If you perform insurance defense work, e-billing capabilities are essential. Most carriers require LEDES-format invoices submitted through specific platforms, making compatible software necessary for getting paid.


What happens to billing data if a solo attorney switches software later?


Most reputable platforms allow data export—client lists, matters, time entries, invoices—in standard formats like CSV. Before committing, verify export capabilities and any associated costs to avoid vendor lock-in.
